question_text: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of fatigue and worsening shortness of breath on exertion. There is no family history of serious illness. She does not smoke. She takes diethylpropion to control her appetite and, as a result, has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the past 5 months. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 115 kg (254 lb); BMI is 44 kg/m2. Her pulse is 83/min and blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a loud pulmonary component of the S2. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's shortness of breath?

                    ### Question
                    A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of fatigue and worsening shortness of breath on exertion. There is no family history of serious illness. She does not smoke. She takes diethylpropion to control her appetite and, as a result, has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the past 5 months. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 115 kg (254 lb); BMI is 44 kg/m2. Her pulse is 83/min and blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a loud pulmonary component of the S2. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's shortness of breath?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Hypertrophy of interventricular septum
opb. Hyperplasia of pulmonary vascular walls
opc. Blockade of the right bundle branch
opd. Fibrosis of pulmonary interstitium
ope. Calcification of the pulmonary valve

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely underlying cause of this patient's shortness of breath is hyperplasia of pulmonary vascular walls due to pulmonary hypertension. This condition can be attributed to both the use of diethylpropion and obesity. Diethylpropion, an appetite suppressant, is known to increase pulmonary artery pressure, leading to pulmonary hypertension and subsequent hyperplasia of the pulmonary vascular walls. Obesity also contributes to increased cardiac output demand and blood volume, further elevating pulmonary artery pressure and promoting vascular changes. The retrieved evidence supports the link between pulmonary hypertension and hyperplasia, aligning with the consensus that these factors can lead to shortness of breath. Other options, such as hypertrophy of the interventricular septum, right bundle branch block, pulmonary interstitial fibrosis, and pulmonary valve calcification, are less consistent with the patient's presentation and the known effects of diethylpropion and obesity.
